content.intro: This lesson focuses on System Catalogs and Information Schema. Its primary job is to help you understand how clients, sessions, server processes, snapshots and storage relate to one another. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing system catalogs and information schema teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: understand how clients, sessions, server processes, snapshots and storage relate to one another. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: System Catalogs and Information Schema
content_blocks.code:
# Python/psycopg 3 — illustrative, not run by the browser playground
import os
import psycopg

with psycopg.connect(os.environ['DATABASE_URL']) as conn:
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute('SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE id = %s', (42,))
        rows = cur.fetchall()
        print(rows)
content_blocks.expected_output: Prints the rows returned for product id 42, or an empty list when no row matches.
content_blocks.safety_note: CodeLeaf does not execute this Python snippet. Never run arbitrary learner code inside FastAPI or a production web process.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Requires psycopg 3, a configured DATABASE_URL, an existing products table and a separately isolated Python runner. Values use bound parameters.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

content_blocks.text: Version note: PostgreSQL 18.6 is the primary reference. PostgreSQL 19 beta/development features are not assumed to be stable.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “System Catalogs and Information Schema”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “System catalog concepts pg_catalog information_schema”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “System catalog concepts pg_catalog information_schema”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for System Catalogs and Information Schema, with an explanation of “System catalog concepts pg_catalog information_schema”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.
